Parent guide
Welcome
This pack is for grown-ups who share stories with a child aged 10–12. Your child reads the stories alone. Your job is to be the thinking
partner: you ask the questionsthat turn "I liked it" into a real opinion. You need ﬁfteen minutes and the three stories in this book.
Each story is a Jurassic English original. You can read it here on paper, or open it in the free online reader at books.jurassicenglish.com, with read-to-me audio and aquestion on every page.
At Level 3 the big step is interpretation. Your child learns to say what a clue means, not just where it is: "On page 4 it says … This may suggest that … because …".
How
to
read
together
When What
you
do About
Before Read the cover line together. Ask: "What problem do youthink this story is about?" 1 minute
During Your child reads one or two pages. You ask the Talktogether question, then: "What might that mean?" 9 minutes
After Ask one of the four thinking questions below. Ask for apage and a "may suggest". 4 minutes
Finish Colour one box on the progress chart. 1 minute
Three
small
rules
1. Ask
for
meaning,
not
only
facts. "What happened?" is a start. "Why might the writer show us that?" is the goal.
2. Welcome
"maybe". Words like may, might and perhaps show careful thinking, not weak answers.
3. Disagree
kindly. You can have a diﬀerent view. Each of you gives a clue and a reason.
The
four
thinking
questions
Every Jurassic English lesson follows the same four steps, the Jurassic Thinking Cycle.
Step Ask
your
child Listen
for
Look
closely (Analyze) "Which detail matters most on this page? Show me." A detail with a page number
What
matters? (Evaluate) "Was that choice fair or wise? What would you weigh up?" A view that compares two sides
Say
why (Justify) "What does that clue suggest? Why do you think so?" "This may suggest … because …"
What
did
we
learn? (Reﬂect) "Where do you see this in real life? Would you change yourmind?" A link to their world, or a changed view
A strong Level 3 answer has four parts: a view, a clue, what the clue may mean, and a reason.
The
ﬁfteen-minute
routine
Read one story for two weeks.
Day Week
1 Week
2
Monday Your child reads the whole story. Talk together on everypage. Your child retells it from another character's point of view.
Tuesday Read again. Do Word
fossils. Ask the four thinking questions.
Wednesday Pages 1–3: one clue and what it may mean. Think
it
through activity.
Thursday Pages 4–6: what changed, and why? Listen in the online reader, then discuss the ending.
Friday Put
the
story
in
order. I
can check, then colour the progress chart.
Six weeks, three stories: The Unsent Weather Report, then The Last Seat on the Night Ferry, then The Voice in Maya's Tablet. Maya's story is printed here as text; itspictures will appear in the online reader later.
When
it
feels
hard
My
child
only
retells
the
plot. Ask: "Why do you think the writer put that in?"
My
child
says
there
is
one
right
answer. Say: "Two people can read the same clue diﬀerently. Tell me yours."
My
English
is
not
strong. Ask the questions in Vietnamese and let your child answer in English if they can. The thinking is what matters.
My
child
rushes. Ask them to choose the one sentence that matters most on a page, and to explain it.
What
you
will
see
After a few weeks most children start to give reasons on their own, use "may suggest" and "perhaps", and change their mind when a new clue appears. Keep theactivity pages; they show how your child's reasoning grows.

The
empty
square
Every afternoon, Lio helped his aunt record the water level beside the school’s wetland path. Their messages went to a class map. Blue squares meant a reading hadarrived. White squares meant no reading.
On Friday, the square for East Steps stayed white. Rain tapped the classroom windows.
‘Maybe their sensor is broken,’ Lio said.
His aunt, the science teacher, slid him the notebook. ‘Write maybe in the explanation column. Not in the measurement column.’
Lio drew a careful white square. He wished the map had a colour for almost knowing.

A
message
with
no
number
A message ﬁnally arrived from the other school. ‘The board is diﬃcult to see. We’re going back inside.’ There was no number.
The school walk was planned for Saturday. Lio had invited a friend who had never visited the wetland. He had described every bend so often that cancelling felt likebreaking a promise.
‘We should wait,’ he said. ‘A reading might come later.’
His aunt agreed that one might. She also asked what they could prepare if it did not.
Lio kept turning the invitation over. The bright side faced the desk.
